20604: The Bible was written thousands of years ago, copied by hand for centuries and then translated into hundreds of languages. How did it reach us, and how close is what we read to what was first written?
20605: The Bible did not arrive as one finished book. Much of it began as spoken stories, songs, laws and sermons that were written down over roughly a thousand years, first on scrolls and later in bound books called codices. For centuries scribes copied it by hand, and while they made small mistakes, they also guarded it carefully, and we now have thousands of old copies to compare. Scholars called textual critics compare those copies to work out the earliest wording; they agree that the great majority of differences are tiny, while a small number of passages are genuinely uncertain and are flagged in modern Bibles. Translators then turn that text into other languages, and chapter and verse numbers were added much later, in the Middle Ages and the 1500s, to make finding things easier.
20606: The Bible was written by many people over about a thousand years, often after a period of oral telling and in stages.
20607: Before printing (c. 1455) every copy was made by hand, so copies differ; textual criticism is the careful comparison of those copies.
20608: The Dead Sea Scrolls (found from 1947) showed that the main Hebrew text had been copied very faithfully for about a thousand years, and also that other forms of some books existed in Jesus' day.
20609: There are about 5,800 or more Greek New Testament manuscripts, far more than for any other ancient book, though most are medieval and many are fragments.
20610: Most textual differences are spelling, word order or slips of the pen; a few longer passages (such as Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11) are marked as doubtful in most modern Bibles.
20611: Which books belong in the Bible (the canon) was settled gradually by use and recognition, not by one vote.
20612: Chapter divisions date from about 1205 and New Testament verse numbers from 1551; they are helpful tools, not part of the original text.
20613: Before the writing: memory, speech and early records
20614:
In the ancient world most people could not read, and important things were passed on by careful repetition. Families recited stories, priests taught laws, and communities sang psalms in worship. Israel was told to repeat God's words at home and on the road, and to write them on doorposts (Deut 6:6-9).

The Bible also mentions writing very early. Moses is told to write a record of a battle 'in a book' (Exod 17:14) and writes down the words of the covenant (Exod 24:4); Joshua writes in 'the book of the law of God' (Josh 24:26). So oral teaching and writing existed side by side for a long time.

The New Testament shows the same pattern. Paul hands on a summary of the gospel that he himself 'received' (1 Cor 15:3-7), a phrase used for passing on fixed teaching. Luke says that many had already written accounts based on eyewitnesses and that he investigated carefully before writing his own (Luke 1:1-4).

How long the oral stage lasted, and how much stories changed during it, is debated. Many scholars think books such as the Pentateuch grew in stages from older sources; others hold that Moses wrote most of it with later editing. For the Gospels, scholars disagree about how stable oral tradition was, with writers such as Richard Bauckham stressing named eyewitnesses and others stressing community shaping.
20615: Myth: 'Oral tradition works like the telephone game.' Fact: the party game is designed to produce errors, with one hearing and no correction. Ancient communities repeated material many times, in groups, with teachers who could correct mistakes. Scholars still debate how much flexibility there was, but the telephone game is not a fair model.
20617:
Early biblical books were written on scrolls: long strips of papyrus (made from a reed plant) or of leather and parchment (prepared animal skin), rolled around a stick. Jeremiah dictated his prophecies to his scribe Baruch, who wrote them on a scroll; when the king burned it column by column, they wrote it all again with more added (Jer 36:4, Jer 36:32).

A scribe was a trained writer and copyist. Ezra is called 'a ready scribe in the law of Moses' (Ezra 7:6). Paul used a secretary for at least some letters: 'I Tertius, who wrote this epistle' greets the readers of Romans (Rom 16:22), and Paul sometimes added a closing line in his own hand (Gal 6:11).

Christians very early preferred the codex, the ancestor of the modern book, with pages stacked and bound. It was cheaper, held more and made it easier to find a passage. Paul asks Timothy to bring 'the books, but especially the parchments' (2 Tim 4:13). By the 300s parchment codices could hold the whole Bible in one volume.
20618: The Hebrew Bible: from scrolls to the Masoretic text
20619:
The Old Testament was written mostly in Hebrew, with some chapters of Daniel and Ezra in Aramaic. Hebrew was written with consonants only; readers supplied the vowels from memory and reading custom. When Ezra read the law publicly, Levites helped people understand it, giving the sense (Neh 8:8).

Between roughly AD 600 and 1000 a group of Jewish scholars known as the Masoretes (from a word meaning 'tradition') added vowel signs, accent marks and notes in the margins. They counted letters and words and recorded unusual spellings so that copyists would not 'correct' them. The text they handed on is called the Masoretic Text, and it is the basis of almost all modern Old Testament translations.

The oldest complete Masoretic manuscripts are medieval: the Aleppo Codex (about 930, now partly missing) and the Leningrad Codex (dated 1008 or 1009), the oldest complete Hebrew Bible. Before 1947 that meant our full Hebrew copies were about a thousand years later than the last Old Testament books.
20620: The Dead Sea Scrolls: a thousand-year check
20621:
In 1947 a Bedouin shepherd found jars of scrolls in a cave near Qumran, by the Dead Sea. Over the next decade eleven caves yielded remains of about 900 scrolls, of which over 200 are copies of biblical books. Every Old Testament book except Esther is represented, at least in fragments. Most date from about 250 BC to AD 68.

The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a), copied around 125 BC, is complete. When compared with the medieval Masoretic Isaiah, the two agree very closely: most differences are spelling, small grammatical forms and occasional words. This showed that the scribes behind the Masoretic Text had copied with remarkable care for about a millennium.

The scrolls also showed something less often mentioned: in Jesus' day more than one form of some books circulated. A Qumran Jeremiah (4QJer-b) matches the shorter form of the book known from the Greek Septuagint. A Samuel scroll (4QSam-a) contains a paragraph about King Nahash that is missing from the Masoretic text but is described by Josephus; some modern versions such as the NRSV include it before 1 Sam 11:1. At Deut 32:8 the scrolls read 'sons of God' where the Masoretic Text has 'sons of Israel'.

So the honest summary is two-sided: the main text was stable and well preserved, and there was also real variety in some books that modern scholars weigh book by book.
20622: Two opposite myths. 'The Dead Sea Scrolls proved the Old Testament is word-for-word identical to the originals' overstates it: some books existed in different editions. 'The scrolls showed the Bible was rewritten' is also wrong: they confirmed that the Masoretic tradition was copied with great accuracy.
20623: The Septuagint and the New Testament manuscripts
20624:
From about the 200s BC Jews in Alexandria translated their scriptures into Greek. This translation is called the Septuagint (Latin for 'seventy', after a legend of 70 or 72 translators). It became the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the early church, and New Testament writers often quote it.

The New Testament books were written in Greek, roughly between AD 50 and 100. Letters were copied and passed between churches: Paul asks the Colossians to swap letters with Laodicea (Col 4:16), and 2 Peter already speaks of Paul's letters as a group (2 Pet 3:15-16).

None of the original documents (autographs) survives; that is true of virtually every ancient book. What survives are copies. Scholars now list about 5,800 to 5,900 Greek New Testament manuscripts, from scraps to complete Bibles, plus thousands of early translations (Latin, Syriac, Coptic and others) and countless quotations in early Christian writers.

Notable examples: P52, a scrap of John 18 usually dated to the first half or middle of the 100s (some scholars argue for a wider range, into the 200s); P46, a collection of Paul's letters from about 200; and the great parchment Bibles Codex Vaticanus (about 300-350) and Codex Sinaiticus (about 330-360).
20625: Counting manuscripts sounds impressive, but most Greek copies are from after AD 800. What matters more is how many early witnesses there are, and here too the New Testament is far better attested than other ancient texts, with dozens of papyri from before 300.
20627:
Textual criticism means comparing copies to work out what the original most likely said. 'Criticism' here means careful judgement, not attack. A textual critic asks: which reading is found in the oldest and most widespread copies? Which reading best explains how the others arose? Which is the kind of change a tired or well-meaning scribe would make?

Most variants are trivial: spelling, word order (Greek word order is flexible), a missing 'the', or a scribe skipping a line because two lines ended the same way. Very few affect meaning, and scholars across the spectrum agree that no central Christian teaching depends on a disputed reading alone.

A few are larger and are marked in modern Bibles. The longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:9-20) is missing from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11) is absent from the earliest Greek copies of John, though many scholars think it is an old, true story. The 'three heavenly witnesses' at 1 John 5:7 in the King James Version comes from late Latin copies and is almost universally regarded as an addition. Others include Luke 22:43-44 and Acts 8:37.

Where scholars disagree is in tone and implications. Bart Ehrman (*Misquoting Jesus*, 2005) stresses that scribes sometimes changed the text deliberately and that we cannot always be sure of the original. Daniel Wallace and others respond that the sheer number of copies lets us recover the original wording with high confidence in nearly every place. Some, such as David Parker, prefer to speak of a 'living text' and question whether a single original is always the right goal.
20628: Scholars agree on the facts (how many variants, which passages are doubtful). They disagree about emphasis: whether the glass is 'nearly full' (we can recover the text with high confidence) or whether the uncertainties, though small, should make us more cautious about speaking of 'the original'.
20629: Which books? A short note on the canon
20630:
'Canon' comes from a Greek word for a measuring rod. It means the list of books a community treats as Scripture. Jesus refers to the Hebrew scriptures as 'the law of Moses, and the prophets, and the psalms' (Luke 24:44), a three-part grouping close to the later Jewish one.

For the New Testament, the four Gospels and Paul's letters were widely accepted by the late 100s. A few books (Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation) were questioned in some regions for longer. The first list exactly matching today's 27 books is in a letter of Athanasius of Alexandria in 367. Regional councils in North Africa (Hippo 393, Carthage 397) endorsed the same New Testament list.

Christians still differ over the Old Testament: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include extra books (the deuterocanon) that Protestant Bibles omit or place in a separate section. The companion guide 'Why some books were left out' tells that story in detail.
20631: Translations: from Greek and Latin to every language
20632:
The Bible has been translated from the start: the Septuagint into Greek, then Latin, Syriac, Coptic, Gothic, Armenian, Ethiopic and more. Jerome's Latin translation, begun around 382 at the request of Pope Damasus and largely finished by about 405, became known as the Vulgate ('common version') and was the Bible of Western Europe for a thousand years.

In England, followers of John Wycliffe produced English Bibles from the Latin in the 1380s and 1390s. Printing changed everything: the Gutenberg Bible (a Latin Bible) appeared about 1455, and Erasmus printed the Greek New Testament in 1516. William Tyndale translated the New Testament from Greek into English (1526) and was executed in 1536. Martin Luther's German New Testament appeared in 1522 and his complete Bible in 1534. The King James Version of 1611 drew heavily on Tyndale.

Modern translations use older manuscripts discovered since 1611 and differ in approach. 'Formal equivalence' tries to keep close to the original words and structure (for example the ESV or NASB). 'Dynamic' or 'functional equivalence' aims to convey the same meaning in natural modern speech (for example the NLT or GNT). Most translations sit somewhere between. Every translation involves choices, which is why comparing several is a good habit.
20633: Myth: 'Modern Bibles have removed verses.' Fact: modern translations follow older manuscripts that do not contain some lines later added in medieval copies. Most print those lines in brackets or footnotes so readers can see them. Whether the older or the majority of later manuscripts should be preferred is debated by a minority who favour the Byzantine or 'Textus Receptus' tradition.
20634: Chapter and verse: a medieval convenience
20635:
The original books had no chapter or verse numbers. Hebrew scrolls did have paragraph breaks and, by the Masoretic period, marked verse endings, but no numbers.

The chapter divisions most Bibles use are usually credited to Stephen Langton, who taught in Paris before becoming Archbishop of Canterbury in 1207; they were added to Latin Bibles around 1205. Numbered verses in the Hebrew Bible go back to a Hebrew concordance by Rabbi Isaac Nathan in the 1440s. The Paris printer Robert Estienne (Stephanus) added New Testament verse numbers in his Greek New Testament of 1551, reportedly working partly while travelling. The Geneva Bible of 1560 was the first complete English Bible with numbered verses throughout.

These divisions are useful but sometimes break a thought in the wrong place. For example, the paragraph that begins at Isa 52:13 belongs with Isa 53, and 1 Cor 13 continues an argument that starts in 1 Cor 12. Reading by paragraphs and whole books helps avoid lifting verses out of context.
20636: Myth: 'Chapter and verse numbers are part of the inspired text.' Fact: they were added more than a thousand years after the books were written, as a reference system. Different traditions even number some chapters differently (for example Psalm titles, and Mal 4 is chapter 3 in Hebrew Bibles).
